title: Would You Rather / Estimation
subtitle: Low-floor prompts that ask every student to commit to an answer and defend it with mathematics — building reasoning and the confidence to take a stance.

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: John Stevens, Would You Rather? · Andrew Stadel, Estimation 180 · NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014).

blocks.text: Two closely related routines built on the same move: **everyone commits, then justifies with mathematics.**

items: **Would You Rather?** — two options are offered (“Would you rather have 30% off a $50 jacket, or $20 off?”). Students pick and *justify with math*. There’s often no single right answer — the reasoning is the point.
**Estimation** — a quantity is shown and students give a estimate, plus a “too low” and “too high” they’re sure of, then reason toward “just right” before the reveal.

blocks.text: Both have a very low floor — everyone can pick or estimate — and a high ceiling, because the justification can go as deep as you push it.

Many students have learned to wait for the “right way” before committing. These routines flip that: you commit *first*, then reason. There’s no single right answer to fear, so students who doubt themselves in math get a safe, genuine way to take a mathematical stance — which is how productive disposition grows.

blocks.label: Effective Teaching Practices
items: Implement tasks that promote reasoning
Pose purposeful questions
Facilitate meaningful discourse
**Pose the prompt** — two options, or a quantity to estimate.
**Everyone commits.** Pick a side, or write an estimate plus a too-low / too-high. No fence-sitting — commitment is the entry.
**Justify with math.** Turn-and-talk: “Why? What’s your mathematical reason?”
**Share & debate.** Hear competing justifications; a student may change their mind — celebrate that.
**Resolve (or reveal).** For estimation, reveal the actual; for Would You Rather, settle what the math says (and where it depends on assumptions).

blocks.text: What it looks and sounds like

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: Every student committed to a choice/estimate
“I picked this because the math shows…”
Students changing their mind from a good argument
Reasonable bounds (“it can’t be less than…”)

no.title: We should not see
items: Choices with no mathematical justification
Students waiting for the “right” answer before committing
Only confident students participating
Treating estimation as “just guessing”
**The lowest floor of any routine** — everyone can pick a side or give a number, so participation is universal before reasoning deepens.
**No single right answer** removes the fear of being wrong — especially powerful for students with math anxiety.
**Real-world contexts** (shopping, sports, food) invite students’ lived experience and can reflect their communities.
**Sentence stems** (“I’d rather ___ because ___”) support multilingual learners in justifying.

blocks.text: Free prompt libraries exist (wouldyourather.math · Estimation 180). Choose a prompt where the math genuinely decides it — or where it interestingly *depends* on an assumption, which makes for the best debate.

blocks.text: Where it lives in the lesson
An **Opener routine** — reach for it when your purpose is to **spark reasoning and build disposition**, or to hook a topic with a real, arguable question.

Choose Would You Rather / Estimation when you want maximum participation and a low-risk entry — especially early in building a discourse culture, or to launch a unit (a percent-discount prompt before a lesson on percents). The justification is where the mathematics lives.

blocks.title: The move that makes it mathematical

blocks.text: The pick or the estimate is just the hook. The learning is in **“why — with math?”** Without the justification press, it’s a fun guess; with it, students are reasoning about rates, percents, and quantities and defending a position. Always push from the choice to the math.

items: **Everyone commits first** — a show of hands, a written estimate, a side. No one opts out; commitment is the entry ticket.
**Justify before sharing:** turn-and-talk, “what’s your mathematical reason?”
**Surface competing arguments** and let the class weigh them.
**For estimation:** collect too-low / too-high bounds, then “just right,” then reveal — and discuss whose reasoning got closest and why.
**Name what mathematics decided it** (or what assumption it depended on).

rows: Would you rather have **30% off a $50 jacket** or **$20 off**?
Percent of a quantity; comparing absolute vs. relative discount.
Would you rather run **3 miles in 24 min** or **5 miles in 42 min** (which pace is faster)?
Would you rather have **2/3 of a pizza** or **5/8 of a pizza**?
Estimate: **how many basketballs fill the doorway?** Too low? Too high?
Would you rather get **$1 doubled for 10 days** or **$100/day for 10 days**?
Estimate: **what % of this grid is shaded?**

blocks.title: Pick prompts the math actually decides

blocks.text: The best Would You Rather prompts are ones where reasoning produces a clear winner — or where it interestingly *depends* (on how big the purchase is, on your pace goal). “It depends, and here’s the math” is a sophisticated, satisfying place to land.

items: **Commit-first guarantees participation** from every student before any reasoning is shared aloud.
**Choose contexts that reflect your students** — their interests and communities — so the math connects to lived experience.
**Post justification stems** (“I’d rather ___ because the math shows ___”) for multilingual learners.

blocks.text: Committing to a position and defending it with mathematics is exactly the disposition students need for the rich tasks of **Core Instruction** — where they’ll take a stance, try a strategy, and justify it. This routine builds the courage to reason out loud in the lowest-stakes way possible.
